title: How To Make Perfect Smoothies at Home
summary: Once Upon a Farm Co-founder and Chief Innovation Officer, Cassandra Curtis shares her foolproof formula and tips and tricks to blending the perfect smoothie.
body_text: Cassandra Curtis has made more smoothies than she can count. As Once Upon a Farm's Co-founder and resident smoothie expert, she knows exactly what separates a great blend from a mediocre one. She's sharing her full playbook, along with a printable cheat sheet for your fridge. The Core Elements of a Perfect Smoothie Building a great smoothie is all about balance—great flavor, plenty of nutrition, a vibrant color, and a creamy texture. "The best smoothies don't just taste 'healthy,'" says Cassandra, "they taste delicious while delivering real nutritional value." How To Achieve the Ideal Smoothie Texture To achieve that creamy texture, it helps to start with a simple formula. Cassandra recommends: 1 cup liquid (oat milk, almond milk, dairy milk, water, etc.) 1 cup frozen fruit and/or vegetables ½ cup fresh produce 1 serving protein (Greek yogurt, protein powder, nut butter, etc.) 1 tablespoon dietary fat (chia seeds, flax seed, avocado, coconut, or nut butter) Once Upon a Farm Co-founder and Chief Innovation Officer, Cassandra Curtis Choosing Your Smoothie's Liquid Base The best liquid depends on what you're looking for. Milk or plant-based milk adds creaminess and extra nutrition, while coconut water is a great option if hydration is your priority. Water keeps things light and refreshing, and yogurt adds protein, probiotics, and an extra-thick texture. "Start with about one cup of liquid per serving," Cassandra advises. "You can always add more, but it's much harder to fix a smoothie that's too thin." Best Fruits for Blending Some fruits naturally create a smooth, creamy consistency. Cassandra's favorites include bananas, mangoes, peaches, and avocado, all of which blend beautifully and add richness without overpowering the flavor. A few fruits can be a little trickier. Apples and pears can taste gritty if they aren't blended thoroughly, while pineapple can leave behind fibrous pieces, and blackberries and raspberries are delicious, but their seeds may create a slightly grainier texture. Best Veggies for Smoothies Vegetables are one of the easiest ways to boost the nutritional value of a smoothie without changing the flavor too much. Cassandra recommends starting with mild vegetables that blend smoothly and let the fruit shine. Spinach, baby kale, cauliflower, zucchini, cooked sweet potato, cucumber, and carrots are all great options. Some vegetables need a lighter touch. Raw broccoli, Brussels sprouts, beets, and stronger greens like mustard greens can quickly take over the flavor. "These vegetables can add bitterness or earthy flavors pretty quickly," she says. "A small amount can work well, but balance is key." Use These Ingredients Sparingly Some ingredients pack a lot of flavor, so a little goes a long way. Fresh ginger, turmeric, spirulina, matcha, mint, raw cacao, nutmeg, and clove can all add depth, but they're best added gradually. "It's always easier to add more than it is to take it away," Cassandra says. Free Printable Smoothie-Making Guide Download and print out our free guide to keep on your fridge for smoother blending! Printing Instructions: Click this link to download PDF file . Print the file in color or black and white. Frozen vs. Fresh: Does It Matter? Both frozen and fresh ingredients deserve a place in your smoothie recipes. Using a combination of both gives you the best balance of freshness and creaminess. Frozen: Bananas, mangoes, berries, peaches, pineapple, and even cauliflower are ideal because they create a thick, frosty texture without relying on ice, which can water down flavor. Fresh: Leafy greens, herbs, citrus, cucumber, and avocado work best, as brightness and texture matter most. Prep These Before Blending Most smoothie ingredients are low-maintenance. Berries, spinach, baby kale, cucumbers, and zucchini can usually go straight into the blender. A few fruits require a little prep first: Remove the peel from citrus, the pit from mangoes and avocados, and the skin and core from pineapple. Apples, pears, and peaches can often be blended with their skins after removing the pits or seeds. While the skin creates a slightly more fibrous texture, it contains prebiotic fiber, so it's worth keeping! How to Use Protein Powders and Functional Add-Ins Protein powders, greens powders, and other functional add-ins can boost nutrition, but more isn't always better. Cassandra recommends starting with about half of the suggested serving, then tasting before adding more. Stronger-flavored powders tend to pair well with naturally sweet fruits like bananas and mangoes. If your protein powder is already sweetened, consider using fruits that are a little less sweet to keep everything balanced. "Think of these ingredients as supporting players," she says, "not the whole smoothie." Pro Tips Skip the ice. Frozen fruit chills while adding flavor. Start with less liquid. It’s easier to thin out a smoothie than to thicken it. Taste and adjust. Before adding, find out what you’re working with. Balance out sweetness. Very ripe fruit + juice + sweetened protein powder = an overly sweet smoothie. Go easy on the greens. Too much can lead to a bitter, earthy smoothie. Texture Not Quite Right? Don't fret! Your smoothie can still be rescued. Too Thick: Add a few tablespoons of liquid until you reach your desired consistency. Too Thin: Add frozen banana, mango, or cauliflower. Greek yogurt or soaked chia seeds can help, too. Too Grainy: Blend longer, or add a creamy ingredient like banana, avocado, or yogurt.

title: Legacy in Motion: Jim Clapper Visits St Andrews, Honouring a Century of Innovation
body_text: Change Language If you are a customer with a product-related inquiry, please contact us at www.toro.com/customer-support/contact . If you are a member of the media, please contact the appropriate individual shown below: Legacy in Motion: Jim Clapper Visits St Andrews, Honouring a Century of Innovation Oct 01, 2025 | Golf ST ANDREWS, Scotland. (October, 2025) — In a moment that bridges history and innovation, Jim Clapper was recently photographed at the iconic Old Course at St Andrews Links, seated atop a Toro® Greensmaster® eTriflex® 3370. A machine whose origins trace back to his great-grandfather, John Samuel Clapper, co-founder and first president of Toro. The Greensmaster eTriflex 3370, an all-electric greens mower, is a modern embodiment of a visionary patent filed decades ago by John Samuel Clapper. His original design was revolutionary for its time, featuring tractor-mounted electric-powered cutting reels and a host of forward-thinking features: Curved Precision : Closely spaced rows of cutting units allowed for seamless movement around curves, eliminating uncut strips and protecting turf integrity. Grass Catcher Integration : Each cutting unit could be equipped with a catcher without altering spacing — a nod to both efficiency and cleanliness. Modular Versatility : The mower supported configurations from one to five cutting units, all easily detachable for flexible use. Simplified Lifting Mechanism : Operators could lift individual cutters off the ground to facilitate turning and transport without engaging the blades. Clapper’s invention was showcased at traveling manufacturer exhibitions, generating buzz across the golf industry. The Detroit News hailed it as “one of the most advanced ideas in mowers.” Yet, despite its ingenuity, the corded design and reliance on portable generators limited its commercial success, clean energy simply wasn’t in demand at the time. Sandy Reid, Director of Greenkeeping at St Andrews Links Trust, shared his thoughts on the partnership and the Greensmaster eTriflex 3370: “Our longstanding partnership with Toro has been built on shared values of quality, innovation, and a commitment to excellence on the golf course. The Greensmaster eTriflex 3370 is a perfect example of this, combining precision cutting, ease of use, and an excellent operator experience. Across our seven courses at St Andrews Links, we utilise ten 3370 units to cut greens, tees, and surrounds to the highest standards. This includes the cutting of greens during the 150th Open, the Walker Cup, and the AIG Women’s Open. Toro’s commitment to quality is unsurpassed, and the 3370 helps us consistently deliver world-class playing surfaces.” Today, the Greensmaster 3370 stands as a tribute to that early vision. Jim Clapper’s visit to St Andrews not only celebrates his family’s legacy but also highlights Toro’s enduring commitment to innovation and sustainability — values that have defined its 25-year relationship with St Andrews Links. title: Why pipeline integrity management demands more than most GIS software delivers
summary: Pipeline integrity management requires handling scale, regulation, connectivity, and crew skill gaps all at once.
body_text: Pipeline integrity teams manage corridors spanning hundreds of miles under strict federal repair deadlines. Connectivity gaps and crew expertise gaps compound the challenge in the field. Most software wasn’t built to handle scale, regulation, connectivity, and crew skill gaps together. Here’s what pipeline integrity software needs to deliver instead. Key insights Pipeline corridors stretch across multiple states, and coordinate accuracy has to hold up across every mile. Regulatory deadlines for anomaly repair are strict, and they depend entirely on accurate location and severity data. Many pipeline corridors and well pads sit far from reliable cell coverage for extended stretches. Pipeline technicians and right-of-way agents bring deep expertise in corrosion, coatings, and easements, even without formal GIS training. Software built to handle scale, regulation, connectivity, and crew expertise together reduces field friction significantly. Pipeline integrity work is some of the hardest spatial data collection in any industry. Corridors stretch for hundreds of miles, crews lose cell signal for long stretches at a time, and regulators still expect airtight records regardless. Right-of-way agents and pipeline integrity engineers manage coordinate data that has to withstand regulatory review and stay reliable months or years later. Scale, regulatory consequence, connectivity, and crew expertise gaps define this job. They’re the reason field crews need tools built for all four. The scale problem: corridors measured in hundreds of miles Pipeline corridors stretch for hundreds of miles across multiple states and jurisdictions, and every mile carries its own coordinate data, easement records, and inspection history. Oil pipeline inspection work happens across that entire footprint, often in terrain with limited paved access. Crews travel long distances to reach individual valve sites, confirm GPS locations against aging records , and document conditions before making the same trip back. Covering that much ground with reliable spatial data is a different scale of problem than a single facility or service area. Oil and gas field data collection at this scale means treating every mile as its own dataset. Upstream operators face the same scale problem in a different shape. Well pad sites often sit well outside populated areas, and a single field crew may be responsible for dozens of sites across a basin. Scale multiplies the cost of a mistake. A small coordinate error, on a corridor or a well pad, means another full trip to fix it. The regulatory requirements behind pipeline integrity management Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) regulations classify pipeline anomalies by urgency and assign strict repair deadlines to each category. Some conditions require immediate repair, others must be addressed within 60 days, and the rest fall under one-year or two-year windows depending on whether the segment affects a high consequence area . Meeting those deadlines means knowing where every anomaly sits and how severe it is, all at once. Stakes like these are why pipeline integrity management software exists in the first place. Regulators also require operators to fully integrate all relevant segment data into their risk assessments before determining what to fix and when. Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) compliance software is built around exactly that kind of requirement: coordinates, timestamps, and inspection records that all have to hold up under review. Crews feel this pressure directly, since their fieldwork has to meet PHMSA’s data and repair standards. The right pipeline integrity software makes those records defensible without adding friction to the job, and the margin for error is smaller than in almost any other field GIS use case. Connectivity gaps and skill gaps compound each other Dead zones are just part of the territory for pipeline crews. Corridors and well pads sit exactly where cell coverage doesn’t reach, and the job still has to get done anyway. Software that assumes a signal is always available breaks down in precisely the terrain this work lives in. The mismatch runs deeper than connectivity. Pipeline integrity data requires GIS-level precision. The crews collecting it are pipeline technicians, right-of-way agents, and inspectors, trained in corrosion, coatings, and easements. Troubleshooting a GIS interface without a signal isn’t part of the job they signed up for. Add an unreliable signal to that skill mismatch, and data quality suffers on both ends. Crews may enter coordinates manually, but may not reconcile the records until days after the job wraps and they are back in range. Connectivity and expertise gaps compound each other here, and the data pays the price. Real-world example: Diverse Pipeline Services manages a field workforce with a wide range of technical experience. Using Fulcrum, they capture consistent, GIS-ready data regardless of that variation. [ Read the customer story ] What field crews need from pipeline inspection software Most software built for an office falls apart the moment it hits the field. Pipeline inspection software has to earn its place by meeting four conditions. Works without a signal. Software that depends on a live connection becomes dead weight the moment cell coverage disappears. Offline capture needs to cover coordinates, photos, and field notes for a full shift, then sync automatically once a signal returns. Produces GIS-ready output. Translating raw field notes into a GIS specialist’s format takes time away from the actual inspection work. Pipeline GIS software should send data directly into the systems operators already run, including Esri ArcGIS tools, with no manual conversion step. Works for crews without formal GIS training. Asking a crew to learn a second discipline just to file a report ignores what they already know. Pipeline technicians, right-of-way agents, and inspectors understand corrosion, coatings, and easements better than most GIS specialists ever will, and software built for this job should meet that expertise directly. Holds up under regulatory review. A record that can’t withstand scrutiny doesn’t help anyone when PHMSA comes asking. Federal rules also require operators to integrate segment data into ongoing risk assessments as it’s collected. Pipeline integrity software should produce traceable records that support an audit, risk management, and the operator’s regulatory requirements. None of these four conditions are new engineering problems. Plenty of industries already have software that solves each one individually. Pipeline integrity work needs a platform that brings all four together. Four problems, one platform Scale, regulatory consequence, connectivity, and crew expertise gaps aren’t four separate problems. They show up together, on the same corridor, on the same shift, in the same field crew’s workday. Fulcrum is one platform built to meet all four at once. Field crews without formal GIS backgrounds capture GPS-accurate coordinates, photos, and inspection notes offline, then sync everything to Esri or another mapping platform once they’re back in range. Audio FastFill lets a technician log a corrosion reading or anomaly note by voice, hands still on the equipment. Records retain timestamps and location details that teams can use in PHMSA compliance and pipeline safety workflows. Treating scale, regulation, connectivity, and skill gaps as four separate problems is how crews end up patching together four separate tools. The job only gets easier when one platform handles all four. Built for the job, not the office Pipeline integrity work doesn’t leave room for guesswork. title: When Data Centers Move In
summary: REMAX real estate professionals discuss impact on local housing markets.
body_text: As demand for artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure continues to grow, data centers are rapidly expanding across the country. According to the Pew Research Center, more than 1,500 new centers are in development nationwide . For nearby housing markets, the impact is mixed. Research from George Mason University has shown that in some markets, homes located near data centers have sold for higher prices . However, homeowners living near proposed or newly built sites may have concerns about noise, visual impact, energy use and environmental strain. In Dallas–Fort Worth, currently ranked the second-largest data center market in the U.S., the boom is bringing investment, new jobs, infrastructure upgrades and long-term economic development opportunities. According to Todd Luong , an agent with REMAX DFW Associates, buyers and sellers in the Dallas–Fort Worth area are already weighing both the opportunities and tradeoffs tied to this growth. "Sellers in these growth corridors often benefit from increased demand, as buyers anticipate future growth tied to employment and infrastructure investment," Luong says. "Homes in these areas can also move more quickly, especially among investors or buyers who want to be close to major employment centers." Luong also notes that buyer sentiment can shift depending on how close a home is to a proposed or operating facility. "Some buyers may be hesitant if they're concerned about perceived noise or traffic," he says. "As with most things in real estate, how close a home is and how established the data center development is can make a significant difference." Real estate professionals in other fast-growing markets, including metro Atlanta , are seeing similar conversations. "Data centers are increasingly becoming a part of the real estate landscape, and their impact on residential housing is mixed," says Kristen Jones, Broker/Owner of REMAX Around Atlanta . "On the positive side, they bring infrastructure investment, long-term tax revenue and job growth that can benefit local markets. On the other hand, when placed near established neighborhoods, they can raise concerns around land and resource use, aesthetics, noise and long-term compatibility with residential living." Jones says one overlooked issue is how data centers could affect future housing supply. "One of the less-discussed impacts of data centers is how they affect land availability," Jones says. "In some markets, large data center projects compete directly with land that could otherwise support residential development, which can put additional pressure on an already challenged housing supply." As data center development accelerates nationwide, real estate professionals say careful planning is needed to balance economic growth with community needs. "The key is thoughtful zoning and planning so that the growth doesn't come at the expense of livability," Jones adds. title: Time Difference Between Indonesia and Malaysia Explained
summary: Confused about the time difference between Indonesia and Malaysia? Here's a clear, practical guide to all the time zones so you never miss a call or flight.
body_text: Travel Tips You’ve just landed a remote job with a Malaysian company, or maybe you’re planning a video call with family in Kuala Lumpur from your home in Surabaya. Either way, you open your phone, stare at the clock, and wonder: wait, what time is it over there? If you’ve ever had that moment of confusion, you’re definitely not alone. The time difference between Indonesia and Malaysia trips up a lot of people, and honestly, it makes sense why. Both countries are neighbors in Southeast Asia, yet they don’t always share the same clock. For those who also deal with cross-border money transfers, understanding timing is just as important as understanding currency symbols and how they work . This guide breaks it all down in plain language, no geography degree required. Let’s get into it. List of Content Toggle Why Indonesia and Malaysia Have Different Time Zones Before we get to the numbers, it helps to understand why this gets complicated. Indonesia is a massive archipelago stretching nearly 5,000 kilometers from west to east. That kind of geographic spread means one single time zone simply wouldn’t work. Malaysia, on the other hand, uses a single unified time zone across the entire country, including both Peninsular Malaysia and the states of Sabah and Sarawak on Borneo. 1. Indonesia’s Three Time Zones Indonesia officially operates across three time zones: WIB ( Waktu Indonesia Barat ), Western Indonesia Time, UTC+7. This covers Java, Sumatra, and West Kalimantan. WITA ( Waktu Indonesia Tengah ), Central Indonesia Time, UTC+8. This covers Bali, Lombok, Sulawesi, Nusa Tenggara, and most of Kalimantan. WIT ( Waktu Indonesia Timur ), Eastern Indonesia Time, UTC+9. This covers Papua and Maluku. 2. Malaysia’s Single Time Zone Malaysia runs on MST ( Malaysia Standard Time ), which is UTC+8 . This applies uniformly from Perlis in the north all the way to Sabah and Sarawak in East Malaysia. The Time Difference Between Indonesia and Malaysia, Region by Region Now here’s where it gets practical. Because Indonesia has three time zones and Malaysia has one, the gap changes depending on which part of Indonesia you’re in. 1. West Indonesia (WIB) vs. Malaysia Western Indonesia (WIB) sits at UTC+7, while Malaysia is at UTC+8. That means Malaysia is 1 hour ahead of West Indonesia . So if it’s 9:00 AM in Jakarta, it’s already 10:00 AM in Kuala Lumpur. This is the most common comparison people need, since Jakarta is Indonesia’s biggest city and a major hub for business and travel. 2. Central Indonesia (WITA) vs. Malaysia Central Indonesia (WITA) is at UTC+8, the exact same offset as Malaysia. That means there is zero time difference between WITA regions and Malaysia. If you’re in Bali or Makassar calling someone in Kuala Lumpur, you’re on the same clock. Easy! 3. East Indonesia (WIT) vs. Malaysia Eastern Indonesia (WIT) is at UTC+9, making it 1 hour ahead of Malaysia. So East Indonesia is 1 hour ahead of Malaysia . If it’s noon in Ambon or Jayapura, it’s only 11:00 AM in Kuala Lumpur. Quick Reference: Indonesia vs. Malaysia Time at a Glance Here’s a simple summary so you can bookmark this and come back whenever you need it: Jakarta (WIB, UTC+7) → Malaysia is 1 hour ahead Bali / Makassar (WITA, UTC+8) → Malaysia is the same time Jayapura / Ambon (WIT, UTC+9) → Malaysia is 1 hour behind Pretty straightforward once you see it laid out like that, right? Practical Situations Where the Time Difference Actually Matters 1. Scheduling Video Calls and Meetings This is the big one. Whether you’re a freelancer, a remote worker, or just trying to catch up with family, scheduling across borders without knowing the time gap is a recipe for missed calls. If you’re in Jakarta and want to schedule a call at 10:00 AM your time, let your Malaysian contact know it’ll be 11:00 AM their time. Small detail, big difference in professionalism. 2. Booking Flights and Checking Arrivals Flight schedules are listed in local time at the departure and arrival airports. A flight departing Jakarta at 8:00 AM arrives in Kuala Lumpur at a local time that’s one hour ahead, so it might show 10:30 AM arrival for a 2.5-hour flight. Always double-check which time zone the ticket is referencing. 3. Sending Money Across Borders If you’re an Indonesian worker in Malaysia sending money home, timing matters more than you’d think. Bank operating hours differ between the two countries, and knowing when transactions are processed can affect how quickly your family receives funds. For a deeper dive, check out this complete guide to sending money as an Indonesian migrant worker , many of the same principles apply whether you’re in Singapore or Malaysia. And if you’re looking for ways to get money to your family efficiently, these smart tips for sending money to family in Indonesia from abroad are worth a read. 4. Watching Live Events and Broadcasts Sports matches, live-streamed concerts, or TV premieres, they’re often announced in local Malaysian or Indonesian time. Knowing the gap helps you set your alarm correctly and actually catch the thing you’ve been looking forward to. Tips for Managing the Time Difference Like a Pro 1. Use Your Phone’s World Clock Feature Every smartphone has a built-in world clock. Add Kuala Lumpur and your Indonesian city side by side so you can glance at both times without any mental math. 2. Communicate Time Zones Explicitly When scheduling anything across the border, always state which time zone you mean. Say “10 AM WIB” or “10 AM Kuala Lumpur time” rather than just “10 AM.” It takes two extra seconds and saves a lot of confusion. 3. Use a Time Zone Converter Free tools like timeanddate.com or worldtimeserver.com let you plug in two cities and see the exact conversion. Great for one-off scheduling when you can’t remember the offset off the top of your head. 4. Remember Which Region You’re Dealing With Don’t just think “Indonesia”, think which part of Indonesia. Someone calling from Bali has a totally different time situation than someone calling from Medan or Manokwari. See Also: Time Difference Between Singapore and Indonesia Explained Understanding the time difference between Indonesia and Malaysia doesn’t have to be stressful. Once you know Indonesia’s three zones and that Malaysia sits firmly at UTC+8, everything clicks into place. Whether you’re scheduling a work call, catching a flight, or just making sure you don’t ring your keluarga at midnight, you’re now fully equipped to handle it. And for everything else that comes with living or working across these two countries, from sending money back home to navigating daily life abroad, you’re in great company with the many Indonesians who’ve made it work . body_text: Home » Investor Relations » Press Releases » General SMAC Productions Launches Podcast Network with AMP Media, Expanding Its Storytelling Across Sports, Media and Culture 07.08.2026 NEW YORK, NY – July 8, 2026 – SMAC Productions , the premiere entertainment and content studio co-founded by Constance Schwartz-Morini and Michael Strahan, today announced the launch of its new podcast network, The Intersection, in partnership with AMP Media , marking a significant expansion of its storytelling ecosystem. The network will launch with two flagship shows later this year. Leading the initial slate is a powerhouse roster of personalities whose voices have shaped conversations across business, sports, entertainment, and culture for decades. Pro Football Hall of Famer Terrell Owens and acclaimed comedian, writer and producer Chris Spencer will pair their larger-than-life personalities, sharp wit and unfiltered perspectives to create a dynamic forum for candid conversations spanning sports, pop culture and trending headlines. Michael Strahan and Constance Schwartz-Morini – one of the most successful and enduring partnerships in sports and entertainment – will interview the world’s most celebrated icons, executives, and the unsung heroes behind their success for candid cross-industry conversations about leadership, entrepreneurship, and reinvention. AMP Media will add The Intersection shows to AMP’s’ lineup of podcasts including The Triple Option with Urban Meyer, Mark Ingram II and Rob Stone, Unfiltered Soccer with Landon Donovan and Tim Howard , Throwbacks with Matt Leinart and Jerry Ferrara , Post Moves with Candace Parker and Aliyah Boston , Cousins with Vince Carter and Tracy McGrady and Style of Play with Julie Ertz and Kealia Watt. “Building enduring brands and telling compelling stories has always been at the core of SMAC’s mission,“ said April Guidone, COO of SMAC. “Launching a podcast network is a natural evolution of that mission, creating another platform for authentic voices to deepen audience connections, spark meaningful conversations and build communities that resonate across sports, entertainment, and culture. Together with AMP Media, we’re excited to bring that vision to life.” The network builds on SMAC’s success producing scripted and unscripted content across television, film, digital media, as well as supporting podcasts for their talent such as Calm Down with Erin Andrews and Charissa Thompson and The Nikki & Brie Show . All programming will be produced in-house by SMAC, with AMP Media driving distribution, audience development and advertising sales. “SMAC has built an exceptional reputation for developing talent and creating compelling content that resonates with audiences. We’re excited to partner with Michael, Constance and the entire SMAC team to connect with fans in meaningful ways and create new opportunities for brands through the power of AMP’s distribution and media platforms,” said Rob Weisbord, COO and President of Local Media, Sinclair. About SMAC Productions SMAC Productions is the premium content division of SMAC Entertainment, founded by Constance Schwartz-Morini and Michael Strahan, producing scripted and non-scripted television, film, audio and branded content for a wide range of networks and distributors, including HBO, Prime Video, Showtime, BET, ABC, ESPN, E!, NBCUniversal, DIRECTV, NFL Network, Nickelodeon, Roku, Audible, VICE and Turner. Recent credits include two Sports Emmy-nominated docuseries for Prime Video, Evolution of the Black Quarterback and the third season of Deion Sanders’ Coach Prime , the critically acclaimed documentary BS High (HBO Max), The Coach Vick Experience (BET), The Future Is Flag (Prime Video), It’s In the Game: Madden NFL (Prime Video), Black Comedy in America (VICE), and the feature film The Underdoggs (MGM). Other credits include $100,000 Pyramid (ABC), More Than an Athlete (ESPN), The Cost of Winning (HBO), Snoop Dogg’s Father Hood (E!), Play it Forward (Showtime), The Cupcake Guys (Roku), and Snoop Dogg Presents The Joker’s Wild (TNT). Upcoming projects include a three-part docuseries on Deion Sanders (Netflix); the highly anticipated movie Madden (MGM), starring Nicolas Cage, Christian Bale, and Shane Gillis; and a content slate with Kevin Durant’s Boardroom .
